items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 14 June the Government inte nds to hold the 3-hour debate on the
consideration of financial re views of Crown entities, pub lic organisations, and State
enterprises. The Government also inte nds to make further progress on the
Telecommunications (TSO, Broadband, and Other Matters) Amendment Bill.
Wednesday is a members’ day.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Can I therefore seek from the
Acting Leader of the House the assurance that he will not try to ram through the
telecommunications bill under urgency next Thursday?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: The Government has no
intention of using urgency provisions in respect of that bill at this stage.
Economy—Reports
1. AMY ADAMS (National—Selwyn)  to the Minister of Finance : What reports
has he received on the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: More good news. This morning the
Reserve Bank issued its Monetary Policy Statem ent. It confirms the early signs of an
economic recovery. GDP has probably increased modestly through the first half of
2011, despite the impact of the Christchurch  earthquake. The bank e xpects the pace of
growth to pick up, supported by high commodity prices an d a number of other factors,
including the earthquake rebuil d. Businesses are expected to increase their staff hiring
and capital investment.

items.speaker: Amy Adams
items.text: What are the Reserve Bank’s economi c growth forecasts for the next
few years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is predicating GDP growth of 1.2 percent in the year to
March 2011, 2.5 percent in the next 12 m onths, and 4.6 percent to March 2013. The
expected growth in export volumes has rema ined about the same as the central bank
projected in March. Private consumption growth has been revised upwards. These
forecasts are about the same as, if not slightly more positive than, the Treasury forecasts
in the Budget.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Is he aware that the Governor  of the Reserve Bank has just
confirmed to the Finance and Expenditure  Committee that the only reason that the
Reserve Bank is more optimistic than his ow n officials is the high commodity prices,
which themselves are surrounded by downside risk?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The fact that our terms of tr ade are about the highest that
they have been in a long time is a reason for op timism, and of course there is a risk that
commodity prices could drop back. I think the more important point is that the Reserve
Bank forecasts are roughly the same as Tr easury’s forecasts, which are roughly the
same as those of most other economists. The Opposition’s assertion that the forecasts
are widely optimistic is probably overly pessimistic.

items.speaker: Amy Adams
items.text: How do the Reserve Bank economic growth forecasts compare with
the Treasury forecasts that accompanied the Budget last month?
19228 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Jun 2011

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Reserve Bank’s foreca sts are a bit stronger than
Treasury’s. They forecast 2.5 percent grow th in the next ye ar, whereas Treasury
forecasts 1.8 percent. But I must say that forecasts do not make an economy grow. What
makes an economy grow are the decisions that New Zealand households and businesses
make, and my sense is that they are becoming increasingly confident, but not
overconfident, about the prospects for this economy. That is more important than the
forecasts.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does the Minister agree with commentary in the New Zealand
Herald and on www.interest.co.nz, which says not hing is being done to correct the
current account imbalance, nothing is being done to correct the growing international
debt, nothing is being done to create jobs, and it is time that someone did something?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not, and I am stil l waiting to see what the
“something” is.

items.speaker: Amy Adams
items.text: What is the Reserve Bank’s outlook for job growth over the next few
years, and what measures is the Government taking to support new jobs?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Again, the Reserve Bank is e xpecting about the same level
of job growth as was forecast in the Budget, which is around 35,000 new jobs a year.
That is actually not exceptional for New Zealand; that was the average rate of job
creation for the 15 years from 1990 to 2005. The Government is doing everything it can
to give businesses the confid ence to invest, grow, and creat e new jobs. The indications
are that the combination of positive leadership from the Government and a sound
Budget is helping with business confidence.
KiwiRail—Minister’s Statement
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of Transport :
Does he stand by his statement on TVNZ’s Close Up  on 3 May 2010 regarding
KiwiRail workers that “There will be lots of work for these guys, there’s no doubt about
that, because they do a lot of things well and there’s a big rolli ng stock replenishment
and replacement exercise that’s coming down the pipeline”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, I do; and I also stand by the
rest of that quote, which states “you can’t make these things conditional to the deal. The
point I was making about KiwiRa il a few weeks ago is that the reality is this rail
company has been treated like a Cinderella in this country for a long, long time, with all
sorts of political things about  what it should do and what  it shouldn’t do, which don’t
necessarily”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question was a fairly simple question. It just asked whether the
Minister stood by his statement. He went on to say he stood by the rest of it, but I sense
then he started to get into some political comment that was not actually required by the
question.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, I was not, Mr Speaker. That was the actual total quote.
I was just reading back elements of the re st of the quote. The quot e in the question was
taken out of context and I thought I would read the rest of the quote.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise to the Minister if I stopped him, but I think he had read
a fair part of the—

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: There is a very important pa rt of the quote that I was not
able to get to that is pretty relevant to the member’s question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question asked whether the Mi nister stood by this statement,
and if he did not stand by it, he was aske d why not. The question could be answered
yes. Of course, Ministers are allowed to indi cate where a quote is ta ken out of context,
9 Jun 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 19229
but they should not go on reading forever. But on this occasion I will let the Minister
finish the quote.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The remainder was: “And I
believe strongly that if we’re  going to turn KiwiRail ar ound—and it’s a big turnaround
project—then we actually have to let them make the commercial decisions that they
need to make.”

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Minister regret the fact that as a Minister of the Crown
he effectively gave these workers a guarantee that they would have a job—and they may
have made certain commitments to mortgages and so forth—and today 70 workers have
lost their jobs, in spite of the assurance from the Minister that their jobs were secure?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and I do not think the memb er’s characterisation is at
all fair, as I indicated by reading the rest  of that quote. I cer tainly acknowledge the
uncertainty and concern that the affected workers will have, which occurs whenever
these sorts of changes take place in any orga nisation. However, it is important that we
let KiwiRail make its own comm ercial decisions, if it has the chance to turn round and
become successful. We cannot place requi rements on KiwiRail that we do not place on
any other New Zealand company.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: If the Minister believes that it is important to give KiwiRail the
freedom to make its own commercial decisions, can he confirm whether he or any other
Ministers discussed with the chair of KiwiRail the implications for any of our free-trade
agreements were the contracts to end up with an overseas co mpany versus a New
Zealand company?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I can confirm that I did not.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question asked
whether he or any other Minist ers had discussed it. He answ ered the question in regard
to himself. Is he aware of any other Ministers discussing it?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Minister is entitled to answer it for himself. I do not think he
can answer for other Ministers.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In the light of his comments that KiwiRail does do a lot of
things well and that there is a big rolling stock replenis hment, why, then, is KiwiRail
losing 70 jobs today from its Hillside workshop in Dunedin?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: KiwiRail has a massive number  of investments scheduled
over the next 10 years as we seek to turn that organisation round as  part of the $4.6
billion turn-round plan. So there is a huge amount of work across that organisation,
which I note has 4,200 staff, or thereabouts. Ag ain, it is very important that we allow
KiwiRail to make its commercial decisi ons about individual elements of its
organisation. We do not place the sort of requirement that the member seems to be
suggesting on any other New Zealand comp any. If we want to make KiwiRail
successful—and I suspect that the Greens do, because they are big fans of rail—then we
have to allow it to get on and make its appropriate decisions.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Can the Minister not see th e inconsistency between his
Government’s refusal to allow KiwiRail even  to tender to build rolling stock and the
Government’s $35 million subsidy in this ye ar’s Budget for farm irrigation, and was he
involved in any cost-benefit analysis to s how whether investing that money in the
Hillside workshop would have been better than a further subsidy to the farming sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I reject the member’s s uggestion. We did not say to
KiwiRail that it could not bid for the work. It has bid for some work, and, in relation to
the work that it did not  bid for, it made it s own decision. The realit y is that the Greens
and Labour are playing politics with this issue. They had one big train c ontract when
they were in Government, and they gave it to Korea, to build the Matangi trains. Now
19230 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Jun 2011
they are in Opposition it is suddenly all di fferent, and I think we can call that petty
politics and crocodile tears.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: It certainly was not us.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With regard to the Minister’s approach th at it is a singular
commercial decision for KiwiRail, has the Government considered the whole-of-
economy approach in this issue, and ha s he looked at the Business and Economic
Research Ltd report, which looked at whole- of-economy benefits? Were these contracts
to be let in New Zealand, the benefits would be not just to KiwiRail but to all of New
Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Business and Economic Research Ltd report, as I think
we discussed in this House at the time, had a number of large issues with it in terms of
the assumptions it was able to draw. The me mber seems to be s uggesting rejecting the
whole principle of trade and specialisation to allow countries to get ahead. The reality is
that every country specialises in certain areas and trades with other countries. He seems
to be suggesting a return to Fortress New Zealand, which is fine for him but I suspect it
would not be good for any other New Zealander.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: If the Government really believe s that it should be left to the
market and to trade and specialisation, why does the Government have such an
inconsistent approach? On the one hand, KiwiRail tenders the contract to whomever; on
the other hand, when it comes to intensive agriculture and irrigation, the Government
has very, very large subsidies to that industry.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do not see the connection. Obviously, Mr Parker and Dr
Norman got together at lunchtime and cooked that one up. I do not see the connection at
all. What I can tell members once again is that it is very important that politicians stop
making political demands on what is a struggl ing organisation, so that we can turn it
round and make it a success in New Zealand.
Parents Inc.—Funding
3. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister: Has
he given Parents Inc. an undertaking to give them money?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Prime Minister:
No.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, on what did he base his comments before
the election that Parents Inc. delivered fantastic results and he was going to “make sure
they get some money to run their programmes far and wide,”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will appreciate that those comments were made
by the Prime Minister in his capacity as the then Leader of the Opposition. But he has
made no secret of his support, which I share, for a group that has for the last 15 years
educated parents and communities up and down this country, in courses attended by
very large numbers of people.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What discussions did he have with the Minister of Finance
about providing funding to Parents Inc., and why was this orga nisation singled out
before the election as worthy of funding by the then Leader of the Opposition, even
before an application was made?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There were no discussions with the Minister of Finance. In
fact, the decision was made in the Ministry  of Social Development, I presume with
some attention from the Minister for So cial Development and Employment. It is
actually not unusual at all for decisions to be made to contract social service providers
without going through the Ministry of Economic Development tendering system.
9 Jun 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 19231

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did the Government approve $2.4 million untendered to
Parents Inc. for a parenti ng programme, when the evalua tion of it was not completed
and the complete sample, which was to be provided by December 2010, was never
compiled or received?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That decision was made with in the Ministry of Social
Development. But I am interested that th e Labour Party just ha tes anyone who goes out
and talks to New Zealanders in a way that is not—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question asked why a certain  decision was made; it did not
actually invite an answer on whom the Labour Party hates or loves. That is not in order.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did the Government—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I expect the House to extend some courtesy.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did the Government use an incomplete evaluation—one
that had such a low response from parent s using the parenting programme—as its
justification for giving $2.4 million to Parent s Inc., which the Minister for Social
Development and Employment did earlier this month?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That member will know, because she was a Minister in the
previous Government, that most Government spending is not fully evaluated. A lot of it
might struggle to pass an objective evaluati on according to any particular measure of
political correctness that the Labour Party mi ght apply to it. The fact is that this
organisation has for 15 years educated pa rents around New Zealand in very large
numbers. It probably has a better track record on pare nting education than any
organisation in the rest of the country.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that the research ers his Government relied on in
handing over the $2.4 million of taxpayers’ money, untendered, had such a low
response from the survey of parents that th ey decided they needed to incentivise the
parents by offering them either a 16-piece Maxw ell and Williams fine bone china teaset
or three books, but they still failed to complete the sample?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Is the Opposition now saying that the researchers were
stupid, or that there is some thing wrong with the course? I think they need to make up
their minds. But I invite the Opposition to go to any suburb of Hamilton or Palmerston
North and tell people they think that Pare nts Inc. gets it al l wrong. In fact, that
organisation would be regarded as a bit more of an expert on parenting education than
the bureaucracy or the overfunded Families Commission.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that despite the Government allocating $2.4 million
to Parents Inc. for its parenting programme, parents have to pay up to $90 a course; and
how many low-income parents, who are alread y feeling the effects of rising costs, will
be able to afford that amount?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Given the choice between believing that member’s assertion
and the Minister, I believe the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Do I actually need to
indicate what it is? I mean, the Minister ha s indicated there is a question about whether
he believes a statement made by a member in this House. Mr Speaker, you know that he
cannot do that.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Power
items.text: It is a regular occurrence for the member who has just resumed
his seat to yell from that side of the House: “Tell the truth. Tell the truth.”, which would
seem to get us into the same territory that he is now complaining about in respect of that
comment.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the matter can be dealt w ith fairly simply. When members
make statements in questions, they risk those statements being refuted by Ministers. It
seems to me that the Minister was making it fa irly plain that he disagreed totally with
the statement contained in the question. He was doing it in a fairly robust way, and I
19232 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Jun 2011
have no problem with that. This is the dang er that members face wh en they put claims
or allegations into a supplementary question in an area of some interest. Where strong
political views are held, they can get strong political answers.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table a paper from Parents Inc.’s website, which
sets out the cost to parents for its parenting programme, Toolbox.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: What lessons has the Government learnt from the Treasurer’s
exercise with the Pacific Economic Deve lopment Agency, which was about giving
money to people with whom it was associated—l essons that have been applied to this
project, which again has given money, over $2 million without tender, to its friends?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Those statements are unbelievable, coming from a former
Minister of a Labour Government. Fancy a Government giving money to people that it
knew—the previous Labour Government specialis ed in it! In fact, the $2.4 million is to
pay the $90 fee so that foster parents, whom  that Government left unsupported with the
most vulnerable children in New Zealand, can actually get some support. Labour should
actually apologise for its record of failure to support foster parents and to get decent
parent education out in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to tabl e research prepared by Point Research into
Parents Inc.’s Toolbox. It is an evaluation that was uncompleted but used by the
Government to give money to its mates.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will get to her feet , and withdraw and apologise for
that last statement. I will not have the point  of order process abused  like that. There is
nothing wrong with seeking leave to table a document, but that last statement will be
withdrawn and the member will apologise.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I withdraw and apologise. I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, we are seeking leave now to table the document.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yes, I am seeking leave.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Will you ask the Deputy
Prime Minister to withdraw and apologise for the comments he made about me?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will not, because the member knows that she made that comment
under a point of order, when she was seeking the leave of the House. That is quite a
different process from answers to questions or any other process, and it will not be
abused.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. What remedy does a
member have immediately when a member is called a liar—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will resume his seat  right away. This nonsense will
stop; it is just petty and pathetic. Members will notice that earlier on I pulled the
Minister up when a straight question was as ked and he went on to make some comment
about the Labour Party. I pulled him up; I st opped him. I cannot ru n this House in the
way that one party may wish it to be run; I have to run it absolutely fairly to all parties. I
stopped the Minister when he started to a buse the Labour Party—I stopped him in his
tracks. But given some of the questions aske d and the implication in questions—I heard
the question ask whether money was bei ng given to friends—I do not blame the
Minister for giving a pretty robust answer. If members do not like to receive robust
answers, they should be careful about the questions they ask.
9 Jun 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 19233
Contaminated Sites, Tūī Mine—Clean-up Funding and Plan
4. SANDRA GOUDIE (National—Coromandel)  to the Minister for the

items.speaker: Environment
items.text: What response has there been to the Government’s announcements on
contaminated sites, and in particular the pl anned clean-up of the most dangerous site at
the Tūī Mine on Mt Te Aroha?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The announcement of the
funding and plan has been welcomed by th e district and regi onal councils, by the
community, and by local iwi. I acknowledge the strong advocacy of that member for the
risk of this unstable tailings dam to be a ddressed, and also the work of the Green Party,
as a result of which our memorandum of unde rstanding includes work to stabilise and
make safe this particularly dangerous contaminated site.

items.speaker: Sandra Goudie
items.text: What lessons have been learnt from the last major contaminated
site clean-up, at Māpua, which resulted in a very negative report from the Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment and significant concern by local residents, to ensure
that the clean-up of the Tūī Mine is properly managed?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is widely accepted that th ere were significant failings by
the previous Government in the M āpua clean-up. I am pleased to assure the member
that we are taking a quite diffe rent approach. The ministry is funding the project but not
managing it on a day-to-day basis. The mini stry does not have th e appropriate skills—
nor is it realistic—to project-manage a co mplex job like this from Wellington. The
technologies being employed have been successf ully tried and teste d, and we have also
put effective monitoring in place. These pr ojects are notoriously difficult, but I am
satisfied we are applying world best practice.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Tēnā koutou e te Whare. Will the Minister consider further
funding for bioremediation of toxic sites, gi ven the successful model of clean-up being
piloted at contaminated timber treatment sites in Whakatāne?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Firstly, I want to acknowledge the very constructive work
of that member on the issue of contaminated sites and the progress we have been able to
make in respect of the T ūī Mine. In respect of her specific question, yes, the ministry
has a contestable fund for assist ing sites like those in Whakat āne, which she has raised.
Funding would be considered on merit, relativ e to other applications. In terms of any
specific technology, I would need to rely on expert advice as  to whether it was the best
way in which to ensure that the sites she refers to remain safe.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Kia ora t ātou. Was the pentachlorophenol  poisoning and E. coli
in Rotorua’s Puarenga Stream include d in the Government’s announcement on
contaminated sites; if not, what action will the Minister take to ensure this issue is
addressed?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member has raised, as he did in my recent visit to
Rotorua, the specific issues of that stream . That is more majorly an issue of water
quality, and there are some tec hnical questions as to where the source of contamination
is coming from: whether it is the previous  timber treatment site  up the catchment,
whether it is the previous sewerage works, or whether there are other activities in that
catchment that are causing it. When we get the technical advice from Environment Bay
of Plenty as to the source of that cont amination, we will decide whether it is a
contaminated site or whether we have a water clean-up issue on our hands.
Budget 2011—Early Childhood Education
5. Hon HEATHER ROY (ACT)  to the Minister of Education : Why has the
Government budgeted an additional $550.3 million for early childhood education over
the next 4 years?
19234 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Jun 2011

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Because the Government believes
that early childhood education is a good investment for our young New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon Heather Roy
items.text: Does she stand by her Budget da y statement that early childhood
education funding would focus on “increasing part icipation for M āori, Pasifika, and
children from low-income families,”; if so, what is her best estimate of likely increases
in participation rates for these groups from the extra half a billion dollars in funding?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon Heather Roy
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question required much
more than a yes or no answer, I would have thought.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In fairness, the member asked wh ether the Minister could confirm,
if I recollect correctly, that money was being allocated to certain groups, and then the
member went on to ask, if that was so, how  many children would benefit from it. The
Minister, as she is entitled to do, answered th e first part of the question. She said yes,
that the funding was being targeted to  those groups. The member has further
supplementary questions should she wish to use them.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: How does her Government’s fu nding of early childhood education
compare with the 1 percent of GDP spen t on average by other OECD countries and
recommended by UNICEF?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This Budget 2011 provides an 11.5  percent increase in early
childhood education spending from Budget 2010, even in the depths of a severe
economic recession. I think that is an outstanding record from this Government.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Spea ker. The question was quite specific.
It was about the percentage of GDP spent on early childhood education.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will allow the member to repeat her question just to be certain,
because I did not hear it clearly.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: How does her Government’s fu nding of early childhood education
compare with the 1 percent of GDP spen t on average by other OECD countries and
recommended by UNICEF?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: If the member had put that question on notice, I could have
found the percentage for New Zealand. However, I repeat that Budget 2011 provided an
11.5 percent increase over Budget 2010, even in the depths of an economic recession. I
think that is an outstanding record.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Why will early childhood education services that were paid $13.35
per hour per child under 2 years of age, pr ior to her Government ’s funding cuts on 1
February this year, now receive only $11.93 per hour pe r child after her funding
increase on 1 July, which is a funding reduction of $1.42 per hour per child?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: That member continues to misrepresent that this
Government has cut early childhood educati on spending. In fact, th is Government has
continued to increase early childhood educa tion spending. However, we did remove the

7. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Communications and

items.speaker: Information Technology
items.text: What benefits will ultra-fast broadband services bring to
health providers in New Zealand?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): Health care services will make huge gains with the roll-out of ultra-fast
broadband, which is why we are committed to  providing fibre access to all registered
health care centres in urban areas by the end of 2015. Faster  connections will make the
transfer of information and services mu ch simpler and will reduce the tyranny of
distance. By being able to de liver health services in ne w and innovative ways, we will
be able to increase the quality of care th at patients receive and reduce the costs of
providing that care.

items.text: What specific services will be able to be delivered over fibre in the
future that cannot be delivered today?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is very exciting. Ultra-fa st broadband will  give medical
practitioners, wherever their patients are, access to the country’s and the world’s leading
researchers and specialists. Telehealth technologies will allow patients and medical staff
to remotely monitor their hea lth at home, whether it is diagnostic equipment connected
to the hospital or consultati ons conducted in high-definiti on video. Another enormous
benefit will be the ability to transfer me dical files—for example, magnetic resonance
imaging scans—at almost real time, rather th an relying on slow downloads or a courier,
which will save time, money, and, ultimately, lives.

dimethyltryptamine (DMT). DMT is a hallucinogenic drug similar in its effects to LSD.

12. CLARE CURRAN (Lab our—Dunedin South) to the Minister of Transport :

question on the same quote, yes, and, in pa rticular, the full quote, which I will abridge
