items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Has he apologised?

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: He has apologised.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, is that not good? What a smart young man. He is
widely regarded as a smart young man ar ound the building, I understand—a bit of a
mover. But until they apologise—

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: Chris Carter?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, he will never apologise. He never will. At least he has
realised that being in the La bour Party is bad even for his image—even for his image,
being in the Labour Party is a bad look. So he has got out.
But, no, Labour members need to apologise first for the damage that they wreaked on
the New Zealand economy. Thousands of people lost their jobs because of bad
economic management. People’s incomes and we ll-being were reliant  on a speculative
economy driven by the fuel of borrowed money. That was actually Labour’s
contribution to wealth in New Zealand. So those members have to apologise for that.
Then they have to apologise for getting so  out of touch with New Zealand voters that
they forgot that the economy  matters to voters. Labour was chucked out because its
members thought that the things that mattered to Labour mattered to New Zealand. And
they still do. They still think that the things that matter to the Labour Party in
Parliament—which is dominated by studen t politicians, and which is increasingly
behaving like the executive of some worn- out student union—matter to New Zealand.
The reason we know that is th at those members keep whee ling out the same old stuff
that they said when they were in Government.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: And filibustering on a bill for students.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, that is what proves it, actually. There is the one thing
they have been really motivated about in this whole Parliament. I know that it matters to
New Zealand because it fills the halls in Balclutha—I can tell the House that! If a
speaker goes to west Auckland to campai gn on voluntary student union membership,
even Tau Henare could get a crowd! The only thing that really matters to Labour
members is to stop student union membersh ip becoming voluntary. It is the only area
where they have shown any focus, any or ganisation, any backbone, or any leadership—
from the real leader of the Labour caucus, Trevor Mallard. And there is that rising
star—what is his name—from Wellington Central; I cannot remember his name. All I
know is that I used to  think that Ruth Dyson was a hope less health spokesperson, but I
have changed my mind because he has mana ged something that is almost impossible—
that is, to make Ruth Dyson look right on to it when it comes to health. He has
9 Jun 2011 Budget Debate 19261
succeeded. We will wait for “Stuart Little ”—yes—“Andrew Nash”, who plans to win
the Napier seat, does he? So the Labour Party has not hit rock-bottom yet.

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I know these debates are to

items.text: The Budget debate demonstrates that until Labour members
apologise, no one will listen to them.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: So say sorry.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Until they say sorry to the c ountry for all the trouble they
have put us through—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Say sorry for what?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is it— “sorry for what?”. I rest my case. I could not
have put it better myself.
This Government has had three Budgets and one plan. That plan is to rebalance the
economy: to move away from excessive consumption and borrowing and move towards
exports, investment, and savings. There is a very  simple reason for that; it is pragmatic,
as this Government is, under the leadership of the Hon John Key. New Zealanders will
not be able to grow their incomes in the next 10 years from increased house prices and
bigger Government spending, because the world will not lend us the money to do it—
full stop. That is it.  Just about everyone in New Z ealand knows that, except Labour
members, so it cannot happen. We cannot indu lge in wishful thinking here. The world
will not lend us that money, because we are one of the most highly indebted countries in
the developed world. We are up there with Spai n and Portugal. So we will have to earn
it. That is why this Government, over the last three Budgets, has put in place the
building blocks of better economic performance for the future, at the same time as it has
supported this economy through the recession.
I will remind the House of a few of those: in 2009 we locked in one of the largest
infrastructure investment programmes the country has seen in generations. And we have
stuck to it, despite the rece ssion. It is long-term, benefici al to people and the economy,
and the next bit is broadband. In the last Budget we did a tax switch. We increased taxes
on spending and property, and cut taxes on earnings, savings, and investment—the only
thing that Labour had to say was that it wanted to put income taxes back up—which has
changed the incentives in the economy, and pushed us in the direction that New Zealand
is already going. Then in this Budget we got the Government’s books under control, and
set out to lift national savings.
The reason why the Government has been  able to retain the support of New
Zealanders through this difficult time is that we are simply pushing in the direction they
are already going. New Zealanders have been admirably resilient through this recession.
We have not had a national whinge-fest. Th ey have rolled up thei r sleeves and got on
with the job, and that is what the National Government is doing. We are doing what
New Zealanders do. We are being careful with their spending; they did that 2 or 3 years
ago. We want to pull our borrowing back, because they know, and we know, that too
19262 Budget Debate 9 Jun 2011
much of it is a bad thing. That is why we have so much confidence in the future. It is
partly because the trading nations of the As ia-Pacific region want to pay more for more
of our goods—that is very promising for the ne xt 5 to 10 years. Bu t the deeper reason
for our confidence is that resilience that New Zealand has shown.
I am proud to be part of a party that over the last two decades has backed New
Zealand’s transition into bei ng a small, open, flexible, globally focused economy, and
now New Zealand is getting good at it. That is why New Zealanders have not
complained about this recession and that is why they have strongly—

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I move, That the Freedom
Camping Bill be now read a first time.  At the appropriate time I intend to move that the
Local Government and Environment Committe e consider the Freedom Camping Bill,
that the committee report finally to the House on or before 1 August 2011, and that the
committee have authority to meet at any ti me while the House is sitting except during
oral questions, and during any evening on a day on which there has been a sitting of the
House, and on a Friday in a week in which there has been a sitti ng of the House, and
outside the Wellington regi on despite Standing Orders 187, 189(a), and 190(1)(b) and
The purpose of this bill is to address the negative effects of freedom camping. Many
visitors stopping along our roadsides at re st areas and look-outs face more than a
spectacular view. Too often they also face a pile of human waste a nd toilet paper. This
is often a “gift” from a visitor who hired a cheap campervan with no toilet, and then
used the rest area or look- out to camp overnight in or der to avoid paying camping
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19263
ground fees. We are an outdoors destination. We wa nt tourists to continue to come here
to explore and enjoy our countryside. Ne w Zealanders do just that on their own
holidays, and we want to protect our repu tation. Inappropriate camping and toileting
does this country a disservice, and we do no t want this behaviour to be lodged in
anyone’s memories when they get home. Freed om camping is an important part of our
tourism industry and great Kiwi lifestyle, but  we cannot tolerate irresponsible campers
spoiling our most iconic areas with human waste and litter.
This is particularly important as we  gear up for the Rugby World Cup. Roughly
85,000 visitors are expected to arrive on our shores. For many of those this will be the
holiday of a lifetime, so we are acting rapidly to ensure that this legislation is in place
by then.
The number of freedom campers has doubl ed over the past decade to 110,000
international visitors and more than 40,000 New Zealanders. The existing system, in
which each of our 67 districts has its own bylaws, is not working for the responsible
freedom camper wanting to do th e right thing, or for councils wanting to protect their
local environment. This bill will enable  councils to determine where camping is
allowed, where it is restricted to camperva ns with self-containment, and where it is
prohibited. The Department of Conservation w ill be able to make similar rules on the
reserves it manages. There will be na tionally consistent si gnage and practical
enforcement provisions. A website will be provided, outlining where people can and
cannot camp nationally. Camping at specific sensitive sites and depositing human waste
on roadsides is already illegal , but councils and the Depart ment of Conservation have
very limited options for dealing with offe nders. This bill will increase the tools
available to them by creating an infringeme nt regime. This will avoid the need for
councils and the Department of Conservati on to take expens ive court action, and
therefore provide a more effective deterrent to inappropriate behaviour.
The bill will provide the same approach as that used for other relatively minor
offences, such as parking and traffic offences. People can be ticketed when they camp in
an area in which camping is prohibited, or cam p in an area where camping is restricted
and they breach those restrictions—for example, by using a campervan with no toilet in
an area restricted to self-contained campervans, or by depositing waste whilst camping.
The bill sets the infringement fee at $200, and I believe that this will provide a strong
deterrent for potential offenders. Enforcem ent officers will still have the option of
taking a matter to the courts if they consid er that the offence wa rrants that action—for
example, a campervan emptying its sewage tank in a rest area. In that case, a far higher
penalty, to a maximum of $10,000, might be im posed. The ability to impose high fines
already exists for breaches of  council bylaws, including camp ing bylaws, but this bill
provides a uniform regime across council la nd and public conservation land. It will
enable local government agencies to effectively enforce their existing and future bylaws
relating to camping.
I must emphasise that this bill does not change the locations where anyone can camp.
The presumption is still that freedom campi ng is not only allowed but encouraged as a
core part of the back-country experience. The infringement system will apply only in
vehicle-accessible areas near formed roads,  near the coast, and near Great Walks.
Councils and the Department of Conservati on already restrict cam ping where it would
be a problem in specific sites—for exampl e, in city car-parks—where camping could
damage natural values, or where there is a more suitable camping site nearby. This bill
is designed to allow such decisions to be effectively enforced. In the case of public
conservation land, the bill will also provide a clear and tr ansparent method for making
such decisions in future, taking into account the purposes for which land is held and any
management plans.
19264 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
In summary, this bill will provide my depa rtment and councils w ith another tool to
protect our open spaces, our tourism industry, and the interests of back-country users,
and it will reinforce the back-country code. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Conservation is one of those areas that
arouse a huge amount of passion and pride fr om all New Zealanders. What is most
disappointing about the debate that has comm enced is the total l ack of passion, vision,
support, or understanding that the Minister of Conservation demonstrated in her speech.
That will be a big disappointment, as has been this Government’s contribution to
conservation over the last 2½ years.
The Freedom Camping Bill has been warm ly welcomed by many groups around this
country, and Labour will certainly support it s progress to the Local Government and
Environment Committee. I am disappointed th at we will have such little time at the
select committee, as indicated by the Minist er, to consider the concerns that have
already been expressed publicly. As with many legislative provisions, the devil is in the
detail. If we do not get it right at the sele ct committee and report it back to the House,
we are likely to cause problems. The rush, I understand, is to make sure the provisions
are enabled before the Rugby World Cup. I personally do not think that is a good
enough reason to rush legislation and possibly get it wrong.
As the Minister outlined, this provision is  really an empowering one so that local
councils can determine areas where they say freedom camping is not allowed. That is
quite a big step for New Zealand to take . We have often prided ourselves on our
welcoming attitude to people who want to get out and about and see the best of our
country. We do not welcome people who pol lute it. We do not welcome people who
abuse the beauty we are so proud of and dest roy it for other people. It is important to
have that protection, but whether this bill is the right mechanism for doing it is certainly
part of the debate we will have.
I am not sure I agree with the Minister th at the instant fine regime is the most
appropriate, and I do think that there will be more difficult y with enforcement than the
Minister has outlined. For example, if a freedom camper gets a fine and then gets in his
or her car and drives to the airport to leave the country as previously planned, what
happens? Do we just say that that is bad luck? I am not sure we do. The legislation reads
to me as if the vehicle owner has the re sponsibility, but it could be a rental car
company—more likely than not it will be a rental car company. Then what happens?
Does the rental car company have the onus  of passing on the fine that has been
incurred—unfairly, in my view? Does Hertz,  for example, have the responsibility of
chasing that person around the other side of the world in order to  get that $200? That
detail would be quite important, particularly to rental car companies.
Another concern I have is that there c ould be some relationship between motor
camps and a council. The council will determine the zones where freedom camping is or
is not allowed. If there is some relati onship between a camping ground and a council,
the council might say that it is to their be nefit to exclude freedom camping in a large
part of that area, for the be nefit of the motor camp. That would not be fa ir on freedom
campers. They would be unfairly punished because of that relationship. That is
something we also might need to protect against.
Another area of concern that has been  drawn to my attention, through quite
considerable publicity around this  bill, is the issue of tram pers. It is very common in
New Zealand for trampers to sleep the night at the start of the track or at the end of the
track and then start their journey the next da y, either on foot or by driving home. If that
area is not allowed to be used as a freedom  camping area, then those trampers might
have to stay some distance away and ruin wh at is a very important part of tramping
tradition of being able to get to the start of the track the night before and then start
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19265
walking very, very early the next morning. Those are areas that I think deserve the
rigour of attention.
I am sure Chris Auchinvole will guide the bill very well through the Local
Government and Environment Committee, which in my view has developed a
reputation—and a fair reputa tion—of paying considerable attention to detail in
legislation. Our deliberations  today were significantly en hanced by the presence of
Aaron Gilmore, who contributed very well. It was fortunate he was there, because
otherwise we may well have fl oundered on some of the detail,  particularly in the local
government provisions. It was extraordinarily helpful, and I hope he is able to sub in for
some of the members as we consider this bill.
This bill has arisen because of the Government’s desire, which I certainly support, to
ensure that precious areas of our country—are as where people want to visit, see, and
enjoy—are protected against anything unpleasant, are dama ged, or are destroyed by
people who are not as respectfu l as we want them to be. We do not know whether that
happens a lot or is quite rare, but we know th at some councils have been particularly
upset about it. I know that other colleagues will add to that.
Rural Women New Zealand is not a group that complains lightly. It has put on public
record its concerns about the damage to specific environments that is being done by
freedom campers. Mount Maunganui locals have complained of behaviour in their area.
I am sure they were not referring to Sim on Bridges or to any ot her local members of
Parliament; they were referring to freedom ca mpers. That area is a magnificent part of
the country, and I am sure Simon Bridges wants to make sure it is protected, as well.
The same has happened in Queenstown and in Picton. Those are areas where we
want to make sure that as we parade around the world, inviting people to come here and
saying to people that our country is the best in the world and that it is 100% Pure New
Zealand, we want to be able to back that up. When those people come to visit, we want
to show them the pristine areas we so enjoy.
I find it frustrating, though, that the Minister supports this sort of legislation, as she
did in her introductory speech, but at the sa me time has significantly undermined the
ability of her own department—the Depart ment of Conservation—t o progress the very
issues that this Freedom Camping Bill is designed to protect. Basically, instead of
charging the Department of Conservation with protecting our waterways, protecting our
land, and enhancing it for the be tterment of all New Zealande rs and visitors to enjoy,
she has handed it over to Mi nister Brownlee and said he should have a look at the
national park areas in schedule 4 to see whether there is anything there worth mining. In
the most precious parts of New Zealand, she ha s said we should have  a little surgical
mining, as the Prime Minister described it.
I was stunned that the Minister of Conserva tion was prepared to hand over that part
of her portfolio, which should be the area she defends most, to something as outrageous
as mining in those protected areas. Members of the public were outraged, as well, and I
was very proud that we had t housands and thousands of Ne w Zealanders marching on
the street and saying they want  to protect the most precious  parts of our country. These
are the parts of the country that we also wa nt this legislation to  protect from freedom
campers who are damaging it.
I will return to the actions the Minister has taken in terms of the Department of
Conservation. The department is now require d to be a profit-making organisation. That
is not what the Department of Conservation was set up to do. It was designed to be the
advocacy group, the lobby group, and the br ains behind the passion that New
Zealanders feel about their most important areas.
The Minister has led a huge and negative step  backwards in her own portfolio. It is a
big disappointment to many New Zealanders  who care about our environment more
19266 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
than they care about anything else. I was surprised the Minister did not take the lead
when this bill was originally publicised. In fact, it was the Minister for the Environment
who took the lead in all of the media. I was quite surprised that the Minister of
Conservation introduced the bill  today. I thought it had perh aps been transferred to the
Minister for the Environment, for some r eason, because all of the publicity had Nick
Smith’s name attached to it rather than that of the Hon Kate Wilkinson. That is a puzzle,
but I am sure it is something I will spend more time discussing at the select committee,
and I will see whether we can get to the bottom of it.
As I said, the principle of the legislation to  protect our areas that are currently being
damaged by freedom campers is supported by Labour. We will support this bill going to
the select committee. I want the concerns I have raised—and others I am sure submitters
will raise—to be addressed in the select comm ittee process. I am sorry that it will be so
truncated because of the Rugby World Cup. I think our rights to enjoy our country are
worth protecting, and I will be ensuring that that happens.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I wish to take only a brief
call in respect of the Freedom Camping Bill, and to acknowledge and support my
colleague the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkins on. I acknowledge that Kate
Wilkinson is the most practical Minister of Conservation that the department has had in
more than a decade. The practical gains she is making for conservation are far better
than some of the highbrow dreamer ideas we  saw in the years of  Labour. We on this
side of the House are deeply proud of that wo rk. Yes, this bill is a joint piece of work.
The Minister of Local Government, the Mi nister for the Environment—me—and Kate
Wilkinson have worked hard on bringing this  package together, as we should. That is
how we operate on this side of  the House. I know that that side of the House is a bit
incapable of that. I know that Chris Carter and Ruth Dyson do not talk these days. We
on this side of the House work very closely together.
This bill is a very pragmatic response to the real problem of freedom campers
defecating in some of our most iconic spots,  leaving a right mess. This bill provides a
practical response to that. It is no good leav ing every one of our councils to make their
own rules when, frankly, the 120,000-odd interna tional tourists who come here actually
would not know which district they are in from one day to  the next. That is not a
criticism; it is just the na ture of the international trav eller. That is why having a
standardised approach between the Department of Conservation and the councils makes
such good sense.
I commend the provision in this bill for a $200 instant fine for those who breach the
freedom camping requirements. Labour has in dicated some opposition to that. Let me
just say it is totally impractical to say to the Department of Conservation or to a council
that it has to spend 5,000 bucks of ratepayers’ or ta xpayers’ money on trying to
prosecute some tourist from the other side  of the world for defecating at a precious
campsite. It is not practical. A $200 fine is a really sensible way of dealing with it.
I was surprised that Ruth Dyson took issue with the provision that the rental car
company should be responsible fo r the fine in the ev ent of a visitor doing a runner. It is
the same for speeding fines and parking fine s. Do we not care for our environment as
much as we care about those things? We all know what happens. If someone goes to
Australia and gets a car from a rental ca r company, the company takes a copy of their
credit card. If the person pick s up a fine while they are ther e, it is charged back against
them. The most important provision deals with the fact that some rental car
companies—particularly those with rental  vans without containers—have not been
responsible. This bill will put some responsibility back on those companies to play their
part in protecting the environment, and that is a good thing.
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19267
This bill does protect and retain the right for New Zealand families like mine to be
able to go out and enjoy the great outdoors— and so it should. To reassure Ruth Dyson
opposite, I tell her that nothing in this bill will constrain the right of her and her family
or me and my family to go to the end of  the Heaphy Track and camp there for a night
before we proceed to tramp. That is quite plain in the provisions of the bill.
The last point I will make is that the underlying presumption of this bill is that people
can camp anywhere unless a council specifical ly prescribes it as a non-camping area.
Maybe the difference between this side of the House and Labour is that we trust the
councils. We think they are pretty common sense.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Yeah, right! You abolished ours.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Ruth Dyson wants to stand up for the failure of water
management. Only 10 minutes ago she was giving a speech saying she is concerned
about water quality. How can she defend the track record of Environment Canterbury,
which after 18 years did not have a plan in place for dealing with water in the precious
area of Canterbury?
The last thing I want to do is acknowledge Jacqui Dean, the member of Parliament
for Otago. This cause is one she has championed both in Opposition and in
Government. This issue is not new. It has been around for quite a while. Jacqui, both in
caucus and in working with local authorities, ha s been pivotal in this bill getting to this
point. I know that it concerns a particular issue in the Otago area she represents. That
district should be very proud of the contribution she has made to this practical bill being
brought to Parliament to have this environmental problem dealt with. It is a good bill,
and I say good on Jacqui Dean and Kate Wilkin son for taking this practical step to deal
with this environmental issue.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: I take great pleasure in rising to speak on the
Freedom Camping Bill. As my colleague  Ruth Dyson has said, Labour will be
supporting this bill to go to the Local Government and Environment Committee.
This issue is a Nelson issue. It is a big issue in Nelson. The whole business of
responsibility for the environment, and the responsibility of visitors to the loveliest parts
of our country, is one of the presumptions of  this legislation, and I support that. Over
the summer in Nelson this issue kept co ming up. I will give a couple of particular
examples from my own experience. I have the privilege of living just a block away from
a park, quite a large park, in  Nelson. Parked down the end of a dead-end street that
crosses the street I live in have been a nu mber of motor homes and campervans, which
began to attract a lot of pub lic attention for two reasons. One was that up to about a
dozen of them were parked th ere. I myself saw them there;  it was not hard to see them
on my way home. But those campervans were parked there in a place that was not a
camping area. That is one issue.
The second thing is that the fouling of that area really upset local residents, including
me. It is not good to go to bits  of the road that abut parks, where people have stopped
and parked their motor homes or campervans,  and where, if the vans are not self-
contained, they have then proceeded to use the public area as their own personal toilet.
It is not responsible, and it is not what we  want, either from tourists or from New
Zealanders who are camping. It goes for everybody. This bill is about tourists who
come to New Zealand to enjoy our pictures que areas. They must know that it is not
acceptable for them to foul our beautiful enviro nment any more than it is for any of us
to do that. So I support this legislation.
The issue ran hot in Nelson because there was a real concern about the bill
preventing people from enjoyi ng our environment. I hope the Minister of Conservation
has this approach right in the legislation, and we will find out shortly in the select
committee. I think it is about right. The issue is not about preventing people from
19268 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
pulling up, parking, stopping over, and enj oying our lovely environment; nobody wants
to stop that. With the people being called fr eedom campers, though, there was a bit of a
backlash in Nelson, and it was said the bill would outlaw a way of life they enjoyed. But
that is clearly not the purpose of the legi slation, and I would not  support it if it were.
However, we on both sides of the House require people who want to enjoy Neale Park,
or anywhere else in Nelson, to treat those ar eas with respect, and those areas that give
people access to lovely views, water, and recreation in our environment. We do not ask
for any more or any less than that.
I want to give another exam ple that is also related to my own experience. Members
of my family have a place in the Marlborough Sounds. That is not where I live; I live in
Nelson, but it is common for Nelson people to holiday in the Marlborough Sounds and
to go there for recreation. I am one of thos e people, and I thoroughly enjoy it. I will not
tell people exactly where the place is, b ecause they might go there and enjoy it too
much! It happens that in this little bay where my family has a house there is a legitimate
camping site that the Marlborough District Counc il has said can be a camping site for 2
nights only. But the locals have had to put up signs saying “Please don’t treat this like
your personal toilet.”, because the abuse that has occurred in that lovely part of the
Marlborough Sounds has been obscene. It has been offensive in anybody’s language. If
those offenders can be fined, th en that is good. Let us slap an instant fine on them, but,
more than that, let us demonstrate to the people who come to our country as tourists that
we are equipping the local authorities to do something about this issue.
Where my family is in the Marlborough S ounds, as I said, the Ma rlborough District
Council has allocated space for freedom campers. That is great; it is a beautiful spot. It
is nice, and I do not begrudge anybody spending  a couple of nights there. But if their
vehicles are not self-contained, and are not ge ared for the disposing of their own waste,
then I am sorry but they cannot use our b ackyard for that purpose. It does not matter
whether it concerns a park in Nelson or a dear little bay in the Marlborough Sounds
where I am still trying to catch snapper, the protection of the environment that this bill
provides is worth supporting.
I have a bit of a problem, wh ich I hope we can sort out in  the select committee, with
the mechanisms around the instant fine. I think it  will be quite hard to recover that from
campers sometimes, but if it can be done thro ugh credit card bills then that is fine. I
remember a very long time ago getting a fine through Hertz, because I travelled in a bus
lane without knowing it while driving a rental car in Rome.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: How did you know the difference?

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: Well, everybody was going at a zillion miles an hour, so
it was really hard to know. I was just trying to stay aliv e. I did not know it was a bus
lane, and I got a ticket late r on through Hertz for travelling in that lane. But I copped
that, and saw clearly that it is possible a fine can be extracted later on. Billing
someone’s credit card is a very easy wa y of doing that, so let us explore the
practicalities of it.
In essence, this is a constructive bill. I like the fact that it underscores people’s
responsibility. We have a responsibility as citizens and keepers of this land to protect it,
but the people who come to vi sit it also have a responsibilit y to treat our land and this
place with respect, as well. I spent a large part of my youth tramping up and down
Mount Taranaki. I was born and brought up in  New Plymouth, and there we go to the
beach and to the mountain. We learnt that if  we took something in, we took it out; we
did not leave it behind. We should not foul th e environment with waste of any sort, and
the particularly offensive examples we have had recently in the Nelson area have made
me absolutely committed to making sure that this provision goes through and works, so
that local councils and the Department of C onservation have the ability to strike fines
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19269
and to punish people where they are caught. It goes to our reputation as a country and as
a tourist destination, and to our own responsib ility, to look after and be the kaitiaki, the
guardians, of our environment. To that end, I support this bill and so will most of the
people in Nelson. Thank you.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: I am a freedom camper. I spend my holidays cycle
touring this great country of ours, or at least I used to spend my holidays doing that,
when I was able to take my holidays at times when I was not competing with peak
motorised traffic on the roads. Most nights when I am bike touring I sleep in a bed,
especially as I have become older, as it seems more comf ortable. However, when I go
bike touring I always take  a tent, and I always e nd up camping out some nights—
freedom camping. Oftentimes camping is the be st or most attractive option, or the only
option. I guess I pride myself on leaving my campsite as I found it, except for perhaps a
little bit of flattened grass. To me, that is a very valuable part of New Zealand tradition.
Many New Zealanders and, I think we will hear today, many people in this House
value it. It pains me to have seen in recen t decades more and more places that I have
personally camped in and that make really good campsites becoming off limits. Thus,
more and more people are channelled into  commercial campgrounds and away from
being self-reliant.
I also say that it irritates me to see in  the Freedom Camping Bill the term “freedom
camping”, which I think perfectly describe s the New Zealand tradition that I have
referred to, as it is used to mean someth ing quite different. A lthough the definition of
that term in this bill wi ll catch the genuine freedom ca mping I have described, it is
really targeted at one particular group of people: those who travel around in campervans
that do not have toilet facilities and that are,  therefore, cheaper. That is what the bill is
actually about.
Let me be clear. I know there is a genuine problem with that group of people. When I
was a member of the West Coast Tai P outini Conservation Board, we received a
number of delegations from councils coming to  us to complain that almost too many
tourists were being attracted to our regi on by the fantastic West Coast conservation
estate. If any members of the House are not fa miliar with the features of that estate, I
certainly recommend it to them. Councils we re saying that a propor tion of those people
would park their campervans in rest areas and at other points next to the road. There
was both a problem of litter and a larger problem that many of those campervans did not
have toilets. Council staff needed to ta ke time and spend money on a very unpleasant
cleaning up process.
There is a genuine problem, but which soluti on to that problem is most consistent
with maintaining rights and freedoms, and with continuing to encourage our vital
tourism industry? Unsurprisi ngly, the Tourism Industry Asso ciation is aware of this
problem. It had been working on it for so me years and had developed a solution. Its
solution had an operating assumption that, in  general, people come to this country
because of our clean, green reputation, and they do not set out to undermine or despoil
it. The people who rent these particular kinds of campervans—the cheaper ones—are, in
general, some of the most en thusiastic about our environm ent. They rent these vans
because they do not have much money, and th e fact they have chosen to spend their
limited resources to come here speaks volumes about the high priority that they place on
our environment.
Although, of course, there are some ratbags who simply do not care, for the most part
the people who rent these campervans would look after our environm ent if they could,
so the smart approach is to make it easier for them to do precisely that. Put simply,
creating more places where campervans can spend the night that are sensibly spaced and
that have toilet facilities and rubbish facilities is the smart way to go. The campervan
19270 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
companies would be charged with the respons ibility of disseminating information about
the responsibility to use these places, and information about exactly where they are.
That solution was being developed and had not yet been given the chance to work
before this approach from the Government  and, indeed, from Local Government New
Zealand was imposed.
Some critics will say that some local auth orities have large, attractive areas and a
small ratepayer base, and that is a fair point.  I live in one such area, and other members
of this House do also. It is a common probl em, and I know it is a real one, too. That
problem is at the heart of the difficulty of providing good quality health services in
many of our rural areas, for example. It is the reason cited by the West Coast Regional
Council for its being unable to  adequately monitor complia nce with resource consents
as closely as it would like to.
But let us also remember that these tourists are contributing to local economies by
spending on everything except accomm odation. They buy food, fuel, visitor
experiences, and so on from local businesse s. Many businesses benefit directly from
having them in the region, and many others be nefit indirectly. It seems reasonable to
ask that the local economy contribute to some of the facilities needed by tourists,
particularly when those facilities alleviate other costs that woul d otherwise be borne
locally, as they would be in this case.
In cases where a local community still cannot afford the cost of these facilities, the
view of the Green Party is that the Sanita ry Works Subsidy Scheme needs to step up.
The Government needs to ensure that the sc heme is sufficiently resourced and flexible
to be able to assist those local communities to provide campervan facilities. After all,
our whole New Zealand econom y benefits from the t ourism industry, and it is
reasonable that the whole economy, ther efore, helps to provide the tourism
infrastructure required. This is the right a pproach and should be allowed time to gain
traction to deal with the problem.
Instead, the approach being a dopted is punitive. It might work—it is possible that it
will—but it seems a less likely method to work than the one I have outlined. The
problem is that people want  to do the right th ing but cannot do it. More broadly, it
replaces the welcome mat that we extend to tourists with warnings of harsh penalties.
This method runs a great risk of being counter-productive.
In all of the debate, which has been going on for some years now, one of the facts I
find most curious is that there is almost no hard information about the size of the
problem. Perhaps the select committee might challenge officials and submitters to try to
provide this information. I suspect that it is an extensive pr oblem, and undoubtedly a
very unpleasant one, but it is actually relatively small. Th ere is some irony, then, that
this bill is being advanced just now.
I think we established in the House that  one dairy cow produces about the same
volume of excrement as 14 human beings. The Government is planning for a million
extra dairy cows. Despite the Land and Water Forum having provided a historical
consensus for both those who use water, such as the dairy industry, and conservationists
to put in place a national policy statement on fresh water—

items.speaker: Hon Rodney Hide
items.text: They hate farmers.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: —including Federated Farmers, I say to Mr Hide—the Minister
has elected to not include the provision that  would have required resource consent for
dairy intensification. It seems a little ironic in this debate today. The extra pollution that
will be caused by that one decision will dwar f the pollution that could be caused by
hordes of campervan tourists. This bill sets out in the wrong direc tion, casts the net too
widely, and uses the proverbial sledgehammer  to crack a walnut. The Green Party will
oppose it.
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19271

items.speaker: Hon RODNEY HIDE
items.text: I must say I was a bit
shocked that the Green Party has now joined—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: He’s still here.

items.speaker: Hon RODNEY HIDE
items.text: —yes, unlike Darren Hughes—the attack on farmers, along
with the Labour Party. It is very, very clear  that the Green Party hates farmers and the
Labour Party hates farmers. Farmers are the very people who provide the backbone of
the country, and the fact th at those members would turn the issue of freedom camping
into an attack on farmers is extraordinary to me indeed.
Let me start by thanking the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkinson, the Minister
for the Environment, Nick Smith, and their offi cials for their work on this bill, because,
surprisingly, it was a very tough policy issue to work on and to resolve. I also
acknowledge the work of Local Government New Zealand in this regard.
Freedom camping has obviously been increas ing in recent years, particularly in
popular tourist destinations  such as Fiordland, Queen stown, Nelson-Marlborough, the
Coromandel, and the Bay of Plenty. That incr ease in popularity has also resulted in an
increase in complaints. The Greens asked for some data, so here is some. The number of
complaints to the Marlborough District Counc il about freedom camping have increased
from 132 in 2007 to 432 in 2009. The main problem is people who camp on
inappropriate sites such as lay-bys, beaches, and car parks, and leave behind human poo
and other litter. This behaviour  is offensive and it creates a human health risk. Many of
the sites used by freedom campers are on loca l authority or conservation land, and both
councils and the Department of Conserva tion spend a lot of money monitoring and
cleaning up these sites. Queenstown Lakes District Council spends $30,000 a year on
monitoring patrols, just looking out for the poo.
Although we want to encourage visitors to come to New Zealand and enjoy our
country and all it has to offer, we also want them to respect our environment and be
responsible campers. At present, we do not ha ve an effective way to  deter irresponsible
freedom camping or an enforcement regime to address the sometimes offensive
behaviour of some freedom campers—just some. Expensive and time-consuming court
action is not working; therefore, the Free dom Camping Bill provides a low-cost, simple
way of addressing the problems created by some freedom campers. The bill provides a
nationally consistent infringement regime that will enable local authorities and the
Department of Conservation to issue an instant $200 ticket to those who are creating the
problems. This is a great bill, and it has the full support of the ACT Party.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker Robertson. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koe i t ēnei ahiahi, otir ā, ki a t ātou o te Whare.
Kua tū ake au ki te k ōrero mō tēnei o ng ā pire, Freedom Camping Bill . E ai ki t āku e
mōhio nei, ko tōna tikanga he whakarite tikanga, he whakarite whāinga, ture rānei mō te
hunga noho puni nei i Aotearoa. Kei te tautoko te P āti Māori i t ēnei o ng ā pire i t ōna
pānuitanga tuatahi nei. Nā, e ai ki t ā mātou, ēhara i te mea ko te iwi M āori tētahi hunga
whai i t ēnei momo noho. Ko te nuinga o te w ā, ko te Ao M āori ka haere ki roto i te
kāinga o t ētahi o ng ā whanaunga, ehara i te mea n ō te mataku ki te noho i raro i ng ā
whetū, k āo, ehara t ērā i te raruraru ēngari, he momo noho t ēnei e kitea ana, mai i te
hunga i hara mai ai i t āwāhi ki taku m ōhio, nō whenua k ē, ka hara mai ki Aotearoa nei
pēnei i ētahi o ngā kaikōrero i te ahiahi nei, hara mai ki te mātakitaki, ki te āta titiro ki te
ātaahua o Aotearoa wh ānui nui. I roto i a au o Te Waiariki, me k ī, mai i Ng ā Kurī-a-
Whārei ki Tihirau, mai i Maket ū ki Tongariro ka eke mai te hunga t ūruhi, te hunga hara
mai i tāwāhi, i runga i ngā waka e kōrerohia ake nei, ki te noho puni nei. Nō reira, kei te
mārama au ki te tikanga o tēnei pire me te tautoko ake i tōna whāinga.
I te tau kua hipa i te M āehe, ko taku hoa a Rahui Katene, n āna tonu t ētahi kōrero ā-
nūpepa nei i tuku ki te ao, me te whakam ārama ake mō te noho a t ētahi hunga kainoho
19272 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
puni nei i Kaik ōura; me tana āki tonu ki t ērā hunga kia kaha r ātou ki te tiaki i te taiao,
ka mutu, ki te āta whakatikatika i muri mai i a rātau, kia kaua e waiho wā rātau para, wā
rātau tūtae ki te taha o te rori, ki te w āhi i noho ai rātou. E ai ki ngā kōrero i tērā wā mai
i a Rahui, i noho nei t ēnei momo hunga ki runga i t ētahi pā tawhito, pā tūwatawata, ko
Ngā Niho Pā tērā. Kai Kaikōura tēnei o ngā kāinga engari ko te mate kē, ko ngā para, ko
ngā tūtae i waihotia ake ki t ērā o ng ā pā tawhito. Koinei te riri o taku hoa a Rahui,
koinei tāna i tuku ai i tētahi kōrero i te nūpēpa ki te whakahē i tērā momo noho.
Kei te mōhio tātou, nā runga i te āhuatanga o ngā kōrero o te Whare P āremata i te rā
nei, ehara i te mea k ō tēnei kaupapa, te freedom camping  he kaupapa hou, e hia k ē nei
ngā tau kua p ēnei tonu te noho a te hunga hara mai t ūruhi nei, haere i te whenua, ā, ka
noho i te taha o te rori n ā te toringa mai o te r ā rānei, nā te kore waka r ānei, kua t ū te
tēneti, kua noho i te ngahere, i te taha o te rori r ānei. Nō reira, ehara i te mea n ō nāia
tonu nei t ēnei momo noho. Engari, kei te whakarongo ake ki te k ōrero a te mema o te
Kākāriki me tana kī mai, ko t ērā pea ko te aronga o t ēnei pire, e h āngai tonu ana ki ng ā
mea e hara mai ana i runga i ngā whēne, ngā waka heri tāngata nei, ngā vans nei. Koinei
pea t ōna aronga. Ko te mate k ē, m ō tēnei w ā tonu nei, kei te m ōhio tonu t ātou ka
ekengia a Aotearoa e te hunga hara mai ai ki te m ātakitaki i te kapu whutupōro o te ao ā
kō ake nei. Tērā pea ka ekengia a Aotearoa  e te tini, e te mano, e ng ā waka e hia k ē nei,
ā, kāore e kore ka whai i tērā momo noho, arā, ko te noho puni nei.
Pēnei i ētahi atu o te Whare i te ahiahi nei, ko te take nui, ko te waiho ake i te para, te
tūtae i te taha o te rori. Ka p ātaia te p ātai, ā, tēnā, ka taea e t ātou te whakariterite i ng ā
whare paku, i ngā ipu para, me kī, kia taea e rātou te whakatikatika i muri mai i a r ātou?
Koinā te p ātai nui. T ērā pea ka raruraru t ātou ki reira. Ehara i te mea kei a t ātou ng ā
rawa ki te whakatika i ētahi wāhi hei kohikohi i ng ā para, ka mutu, ka p ērā anō hoki ki
te āhuatanga o te t ūtae. Nō reira, ahakoa kei te tautoko ake i t ēnei pire, kei te p ātai te
pātai mō ngā rawa, m ō ngā mea hai whakatutuki i te moemoe ā, kia noho pai, kia noho
ātaahua a Aotearoa nei.
I roto i t ēnei pire, ko te mana o ng ā kaunihera ki te whakarite, i ētahi kaunihera ā-
rohe tāku e kōrero nei, kia taea e r ātou te whakatika i ō rātou ake ture mō rātou ake, mō
tērā rohe, mō tēnā takiwā, mō tērā rohe, mō tēnā takiwā. Ka pērā anō hoki te taha ki Te
Papa Atawhai, kia taea ai e ia te whakarite tikanga m ō tēnā rohe, m ō tēnā takiwā. Nō
reira, he pai tonu t ērā, kia taea ai e r ātou te whakarite i t ērā, ka mutu, m ēnā ka raru
tētahi, ka kore e whai i te ture o t ēnā takiw ā, o t ērā takiw ā, ā, ka p ēnei i ētahi ka
whainahia, mai i te $200, neke atu ki te $10, 000.
Nō reira, ko tāku tino kaupapa, i tua atu o te take m ō ng ā ipu para me ng ā whare
paku hei āwhina, hei wāhi tuku i ng ā para, ko t ērā e pā ana ki te w āhi o te Ao M āori ki
roto i ng ā whiriwhiringa o ng ā kaunihera. I t ēnei w ā tonu nei, i raro i te Local
Government Bill o te tau 2002, kei reira t ētahi w āhanga m ō te k ōrero, m ō te
whakawhitiwhiti whakaaro ki te tangata whenua, ki te mana whenua r ānei. Ko te mate
kē, ehara i te mea he tino pakari mai t ērā whāinga o te ture. Ko t ā mātou e p īrangi nei,
kua whakapakari ake tērā wāhi, arā, kia whai wāhi te Ao Māori i roto i ngā kōrerorero i
te taha o te kaunihera ā-rohe, ka mutu, i te taha o ng ā kāwanatanga ā-rohe—me mahi i
te taha o te mana whenua. Koin ā te tino p ūtake i te mea, i ētahi wā nō te Ao M āori ērā
whenua, ka mutu, me whai wāhi rātou ki te kōrero ki ngā iwi, ka mutu, ki te whakamana
i te wh āinga o t ēnei pire. Ko te mea pai e kitea nei i roto o t ēnei pire, ka waiho ake ki
tēnā rohe, ki t ēna rohe kia whakatika i a ia an ō me ōna ake ture e p ā ana ki a ia engari,
pēnei i t āku e k ōrero nei, ko te īnoi atu kia whai w āhi te Ao Māori, te taha ki te mana
whenua, te tangata whenua i roto i ngā whiriwhiringa.
Ehara i te mea, he nui ngā kōrero i tua atu o tērā. Hoi anō, me pēnei rawa te kōrero, e
kōrerohia ana i roto i ng ā kōrero o te Ao m āori, ko te k ōrero mō Ranginui e t ū nei, mō
Papatūānuku, ko t ā mātau o te Ao M āori, ko t ōna tāhūhū ko te tiaki i te āhuatanga o te
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19273
taiao, ko Papatūānuku e takoto nei. Nō reira, kei te tino āro atu mātou ki te tino pūtake o
tēnei pire. He pai tōna tirohanga, he pai tōna kaupapa, he pai tōna tikanga. Koinei mātou
e tautoko nei i t ēnei pire engari, ka titiro ake ā ngā rā kei mua i te aroa ro, kia kitea mai
ai ko te w āhi ki te Ao M āori i roto i ng ā whakawhitiwhitinga whakaaro ka puta ki te
taha o ngā kaunihera ā-rohe, kaunihera ā-kawanatanga nei. Nō reira, ko ēnei ētahi paku
whakaaro ake hei t āpiri atu ki ētahi o ng ā kōrero i te ahiahi nei. Huri noa i t ō tātou
Whare, kia ora tātou.
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Robe rtson. My huge appreciation to you, and
indeed to us of the House, this afternoon. I rise to address the Freedom Camping Bill.
As I understand it, the purpose of this bill is to find remedies that will deal with issues
caused by freedom campers in New Zealand. The M āori Party supports this bill at its
first reading. However, I need to point out that M āori, by tradition, are not freedom
campers. At most times they stay in the home of a relative—not because they fear
sleeping under the stars; no t at all, that is not wh ere the problem is. To my
understanding, this kind of lifestyle has come about through campers from other
countries coming to see the beauty of New Zealand. Hordes of tourists, and those from
overseas in vehicles referred to here as campervans, have a strong presence in my
electorate of Te Waiariki, whic h stretches from the Dogs of Wh ārei across to Tihirau,
and from Maket ū inland to Mount Tongariro. So I have a clear understanding of what
this bill is about, and support what it is intended to do.
In March last year, my colleague Rahui Kate ne made a widely re ported statement in
the press about the need fo r freedom campers in Kaik ōura to take more care when
deciding where and where not to dispose of their food and body wastes; she urged that
they should take greater care of the environm ent, and ensure that they clean up before
they leave and not leave their rubbish and body wastes on the side of the road or where
they had parked. According to reports at the time, freedom campers were using Ng ā
Niho Pā, a traditional pā site in Kaikōura, as a place to defecate. That so infuriated my
colleague that it prompted her to go to the press to voice her opposition to that form of
camping.
Because of what has been said in the Hous e today, we know that freedom camping is
not a new phenomenon. It has been around for a long, long time. People who have come
from overseas and travelled the land have parked up or pitche d a tent in the bush or by
the roadside at sunset. But I take on board the message from the member of the Green
Party in his address to us, that the focus of this bill is particularly on campers in these
vans. This perhaps is its focus. But the pr oblem is that New Zealand is about to be
inundated by hordes of people coming to wa tch the Rugby World Cup. Without a doubt,
a large number of those people will resort to campervans to get about.
As some in the House have said, the major i ssue is that there are not the facilities to
dispose of human waste and litter left behind  on the roadside. The question then is
whether we can provide toilets and rubbish containers so people can leave the place
nice and tidy after them. That is the big ques tion. It could be our downfall. There are
not the facilities to dispose of human waste and litter. So while  we support this bill, we
question that there are the resources and t ools to fulfil the dream that New Zealand
should remain a beautiful and attractive country.
Local authorities will have the power thr ough this bill to regulate, manage, and
control human waste and litter fo r this or that region or di strict. So that is good. The
bill allows each local authority to set by-l aws to suit its region or  district. The bill
allows for fees and fines to be set from $200 right through to $10,000.
Apart from rubbish bins and toilets to he lp with the removal of litter and human
waste, the real issue I have re lates to the participation of M āoridom in consultations
with councils. Currently there is a prov ision in the Local Government Act 2002 to
19274 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
consult with tangata or mana whenua. The proble m is that that part  of the Act is not
adhered to strongly. We want it enforced more firmly. We want local councils and local
authorities to engage more strongly in their consultations with local Māori, particularly
when it comes to enacting the intention of this bill. A positive feature seen so far about
this bill is its flexib ility. It enables a local author ity to regulate according to its
situation, but, as I said ear lier, participation of local M āori in the consultation process
is a must.
There is not much more to add. Taking care of the environment is  an essential need
to take care of Earth Mother lying here, and Sky Father st anding before us. We support
the real intention of th is bill and its good insight , philosophy, and meaning. The M āori
Party looks forward to seeing a specific consultation provision for iwi, in the bill.
These, then, are but some small considerat ions to add to the speeches this afternoon.
Thank you to us throughout our House.]

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Freedom campers
have an important place in New Zealand’s to urism industry. They are very important to
us. Both international tourists and New Zealand domestic tourists quite rightly enjoy the
freedom to park their vehicles at no cost  and to enjoy our beautiful environment
responsibly. For the most part freedom camp ers in New Zealand are responsible about
where they camp, and they are to be encourag ed in this endeavour. They take notice of
signs that prohibit them from certain areas and they are re sponsible with their waste.
But ever since I have had the privilege of se rving as an MP, I have had people from all
over my electorate, particularly in Tasman, te ll me of their very se rious concerns about
irresponsible campers who i gnore the signs, park their ve hicles in areas with no
facilities, have no facilities in their vehicles, and leave their litter and human waste
behind. In fact, some of the anecdotal eviden ce I have had from local constituents has
been not only disturbing but also, quite frequently, disgusting to hear.
We all know that this problem should not go on. Local councils just have not had the
tools to deal with it until now; neither have communities that have concerns. In
addition, different approaches by different councils have made it difficult for freedom
campers to know where they can and cannot park for the night.
This Freedom Camping Bill deals with the problems I have outlined. It provides
better information for freedom campers and effective enforcement powers to councils. It
enables councils to determine where camping is and is not allowed, where it is restricted
to campervans with self-containment, and wh ere it is prohibited. Nationally consistent
signage and enforcement will make things  clear for everyone i nvolved. Quite frankly,
this is long overdue. I commend this bill to the House.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour) : I wonder what our pioneering ancestors
would think. The Freedom Camping Bill is a nanny State bill if ever there was one,
because we are now going to be told where we can do poos. I will tell members why
this bill is nothing but a bit of grandsta nding by Nick Smith and a few members over
there. If it was a true bill to address the issue, it would be called the “Environmental
Protection Bill”.
I accept that there is an issue and there has been an issue here for a long time. It was
not raised on the basis of people stopping for the night but of people stopping during the
day, and in South Westland in particular.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Doing their business in the day?
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : That is right. I do not think that member does; he
should do it more often, because it might clear his head. The issue is that in many places
throughout rural New Zealand there are simp ly no facilities; ther e are no toilets. If
people are travelling 200 kilometres, or ev en 100 kilometres, a nd stopping, then the
question of where they go to the toilet is a significant one for them. We ended up with,
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19275
and still have, many stopping places—not camping places, but stopping places—up and
down the country that are littered and are absolutely disgusting.
The question is what we have done to help  tourists to know about the situation. We
have done nothing. Our signage is  pathetic. As the Minister  of Tourism I raised the
issue that we as a tourism industry and as a country had a responsibility to inform those
people, whom we were hosting in this countr y, about some normal issues of where they
should go. We tell them whether there is pe trol. We sometimes tell them about the
speed limits. I have to say, t hough, that that signage is qu ite pathetic. Many tourists
coming to this country get pinged for speed ing when they probably have not seen a
speeding sign, because those signs are so small. The same thing will happen now.
The nanny State National Government will let the councils say people can go here
and here, but not there. Speakers in this debate have said the law might be used to chase
people to camping grounds when they ma y have otherwise camped out around this
country. We have a spectacular country. We have a small population. No one could say
we are overpopulated. The vast majority of people visiting this country come because
they want to see the spectacular scenery and enjoy the incredible nature that we have.
I ask what is wrong with using a shovel.  Will someone camping somewhere with a
shovel, dealing with their excrement properly,  be fined as well? Ca n Mr Henare tell us
that? He does not know. The question is wh ether the normal, sensible systems that
many people have adopted over many, many years will be accepted as mitigation for
what has been a growing problem. I accept th at it is a growing problem. But here we
have, for cheap political purposes, a bill that  will, I have to say, send shivers up the
spines of many people trying to market and promote this country to a whole lot of
people out there.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: That was the best the Minister of Tourism could do.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : The Minister of Conserva tion is over there. She is
jumping up and down. I ask her what she or her Government has done to increase the
level of facilities and toilets throughout th e country, and what she will do to address the
issue of daytime toilet need up and dow n this country—up and down this country.
People will be told where to go in the eveni ng when they stop—they will be told where
to go at night—but what about during the daytime? Hold on, hold on! Help is coming.
They will have to go down the road and round the corner, and there is a spot where they
can camp and go to the toilet. It is rather ridiculous.
I think we need a more comprehensive appr oach to this issue. Labour will support
the referral of this bill to the Local G overnment and Environment Committee because
we accept that there is an issue, but I have to say it is a bizarre approach, and it is a half-
hearted approach from a Government that thin ks we can just fine the people who come
to this country—and I can just imagine the reaction of many, many tourists when they
come to this country—when we have not even informed them through a normal system
of signage and education about the protocol s around this. The councils I have spoken to
over the years, Westland Dist rict Council in particular, have been complaining about
this issue for a long, long time, I have to  say. As people have driven down through
South Westland there have been no toilets, and there have been some shocking sights at
popular rest areas. But we have not even put  up a sign. We have not even bothered to
put up a sign that says to those travellers : “No toilets for the next 50 kilometres”,
implying—

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: What should the sign say?
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: Well, just listen.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Go to the gas station.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : We have that. We say: “No petrol for 100
kilometres”. I have seen signs like that. Bu t we do not assist people by saying there are
19276 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
no toilets for 100 kilometres, which would imply the same thing. I am raising the
realistic issues of people as they travel around this country. If the nanny State party over
there is going to tell people where to go to the toilet now, and if the National members
think they have addressed the problem of  camping at night, then they are kidding
themselves. What will this Government do to address the issue of toilet need during the
day, Mr Assistant Speaker R obertson? You can even under stand it yourself, can you
not?
Some real issues need to be addressed here. There are some wider environmental
issues, and the issue of the tourism industry co ntributing to more infrastructure in this
area is an important one. I ch allenge the Government to address that issue. The fact is
that the Sanitary Works Subs idy Scheme—the subsidy for small communities to put in
place toilet facilities and dump stations—has go ne. There is no assistance at all. Small
communities are expected to put in place large facilities. Even for camping grounds that
might be then allocated or dedicated to this purpose, I say that if one has a concentration
of campers in one area, one will have to upgrade the facilities. The question is who does
that. Some commercial camping-grounds w ill be happy to do that, but many, many
areas around this country will not be able to do that without proper assistance.
In conclusion, I say this is an ad hoc response. It is a bit of political grandstanding by
Nick Smith, and it does not address the major issue of infrastructure for tourists—not
just at night time but during the day, as well. If we are to uphold and support the “100%
Pure New Zealand” brand in this countr y, then a more comprehensive look at
environmental infrastructure for tourists has to be addressed. But that Government
chopped $15 million off Tourism New Zealand’ s budget in the last Budget; there is $15
million less to promote New Zealand. I guess that is one way of addressing this
problem, because there certainly will not be  as many people coming to New Zealand.
Maybe that is it—in fact, National might have  outsmarted us; I concede that. It may be
that National’s cunning plan to address this issue is to cut $15 million off Tourism New
Zealand’s budget. It will reduce the number  of people coming to the country, and we
will not have the problem. That is exactly what will happen here.
The bill is a Draconian approach to what is a real issue. We will just fine individuals,
whose understanding of the En glish language might not be  great, who have had no
information or education about the norm a nd protocol in New Z ealand, and who have
hired a rental van, with or without faciliti es—like elsewhere in the world. Those people
will feel really gutted, I am sure, when they are slapped with a $200 fine. It surprises
me, but the nanny State, the Draconian Govern ment that National is, has finally shown
its true colours. It has cut the budget of Tourism New Zealand, and cut the money from
the Sanitary Works Subsidy Scheme and the support for local councils for toilet and
sewerage facilities. It has simply slapped a fine on those people who cannot hold on any
longer. Thank you.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Picture this: an international visitor is on
the edge of the great Lake Taup ō for the very first time, when that visitor stands in a
piece of —. What will that do for his or her e xperience of this fantastic country? There
will be thousands pouring into Taup ō when they come to support South Africa, Ireland,
and Wales during the Rugby World Cup in onl y 92 days’ time. I am proud to support
the Freedom Camping Bill, this practical, sensible legislation that has been led by
Jacqui Dean and the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkinson.

items.speaker: Hon STEVE CHADWICK
items.text: I have listened to the debate in the House,
and I recall that I had a glorious year as a Minister of Conservation. It is a pity that Nick
Smith did not even mention that wonderful, practical reign! However, I am following on
from a former Minister of Tourism, th e Hon Damien O’Connor, who pointed out the
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19277
very problems that we had to face when we we re in Government, but that this bill just
does not fix. This bill is absurd.
Following the example of the member from Taup ō, I ask members to picture this:
new tourists arrive on the shores of Lake Taupō and do not have a clue where to find the
toilets. There is no signage. There is no small subsidy scheme for Little Waih ī to even
build a decent ablution block next to a campi ng ground or at a pull- over on the side of
the road. So what do the tourists do? They f oul the side of the road. We see it, and we
are aware of this problem. But now they will be pinged with a $200 fine. Who will issue
the fine? Will it be the local authority? W ill it be a regional councillor? Will it be a
front-line Department of Conservation range r, who instead of pr otecting species—now
that $13 million is being knocked off the c onservation budget every year—will have to
issue fines? Who will be responsible for i ssuing the fine? Do members know what the
tourists will say? They will say: “I am not going to pay it.”
So we will set up an amazing bureaucracy through the Freedom Camping Bill to
catch the pooper. Is it the dog or is it the pe rson? Who will issue the fine? Is the fine for
the dog or the person? And who wi ll check that the fine has b een paid when the tourists
leave the airport? Will it be a customs officer, or is it the airport’s responsibility to say:
“This person was found soiling the road in Tekap ō, so must not leave the country until
the $200 fine is paid.” This is a stupid bill. That is all. It is not practical and it is stupid.
It is a nanny State response to the comple x issue of the spoili ng of our beautiful
environment, which we all care about.
Freedom campers actually came to us when we were in Government too—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: You did nothing!

items.speaker: Hon STEVE CHADWICK
items.text: Hang on a minute! They proposed a solution with a
mix of penalties for those who did not have ablution facilities in their campervans. They
said there was a problem, but that everyone  was being pinged because some campers
pay a premium to get a campervan that has a good ablution block in it. But is that going
to stop the guy who has been drinking at night and goes into the bushes for a quick one?
We have to think of the pr acticalities around this, and th is bill does not solve the
problem we are all concerned about in respect of our clean, green environment.
There is another issue, and I heard Damien O’Connor mention it  too. It is ironic that
the Government thinks this is the quick fi x to environment protection, when it has cut
the very subsidy that allowed small commun ities to put in basic sanitation blocks and
facilities wherever they saw the need al ong the countryside where freedom campers
wanted to go. That subsidy scheme has gone—zip. I wonder whether the collection of
the $200 fine proposed in this bill will go back into local authorities’ coffers through the
department of tourism so that they can build decent ablution blocks, and campervans
can pull up and use those facilities. That was the sort of proposal and the solution we
put in for other previous big events in this country. We put in more refuse collection and
we started to build small ablution blocks. Members over there did not even know that
scheme existed. I do not think that Govern ment members even realised how good that
scheme was. Local authorities loved it. Local  authorities could make the decision about
where these were to go.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What scheme?

items.speaker: Hon STEVE CHADWICK
items.text: The Sanitary Works Subsidy Scheme. Ask Minister
Tony Ryall. It was administered through the Ministry of Health, and all of the funding
has gone.
The National Government has not even looke d at some little tool  box solutions that
were there for the Government at the time. Clearly, Minister Ryall has not talked to
Minister Wilkinson, who has not talked to the Minister for the Environment, Nick
Smith. Those measures that were already ther e are not even included in this bill. The
19278 Freedom Camping Bill 9 Jun 2011
nanny State National Government is just going to issue fine s all over the country. It is
not going to put up any signage. There is nothing in here about signage to say—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Yes, there is.

items.speaker: Hon STEVE CHADWICK
items.text: No there is not. There is no information for freedom
campers at all about this law change. There should be information kits for new visitors
to the country to say: “Welcome to New Zealand. Now you are going to find you get a
$200 fine, and we will take the apple that you bring in from Aust ralia off you, too. We
will ping you for that. Welcome to New Z ealand. Haere mai. Welcome to the Rugby
World Cup. Have we got a quick-fix solution for you.” This is a band-aid solution. I
hope that the Local Government and Environment Committee can flesh out the bill, and
that is why Labour will support its referral to the select committee.
In some areas, in Rotorua, for example, the provisions in this bill sort of meet what is
being done anyway. We have something cal led a Rotorua open public place policy, and
in that policy we promulgate by-laws and encourage people in freedom camping
situations to go to a place where there is a toilet and ablution facility.
This bill is just silly. It is not a bill that will give us a great reputation as a country of
liberal thinkers. People love the environmen t and people want to come here. It is a
nanny State bill. It is a stupid solution—again, because of the Rugby World Cup. I think
the Minister could have done much better th an this. There could have been a mix of
fines and a mix of the Sanitary Works Subsidy Scheme, and it could have been
promulgated. We could look at where the fi ne could go, instead of just into the
Government coffers as another revenue back-door facility. For goodness’ sake! Who
will be policing this? Who will monitor this? If it is to be front-line Department of
Conservation rangers, then I think that is an appalling waste of conservation money.
There was a whole mix and suite of solutio ns to what looks to be a very overt
problem that causes environmental degradation. I hate this bill being called the Freedom
Camping Bill. To me it is more like the “F reedom Camping is Dead in New Zealand
Bill” or the “We’re Going to Tell You Wher e to Go Bill”. As Damien O’Connor said,
we could have come up with an environmen t protection bill and looked at this whole
problem of degradation and contamina tion of public sites in a much more
comprehensive manner that fitted our clean, green environment.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: The real problem with freedom camping, as
members have noted, is that although the Government can bring in any number of
measures—it might be fines, good signage, or describing places where people can and
cannot camp, and whether they have self-cont ainment—the real problem we need to
overcome is that we need people who vi sit New Zealand from overseas, and New
Zealanders themselves, to understand that th ey have environmental responsibilities. We
cannot stop people going to the loo in our beautiful places in New Zealand just by the
suite of measures we are proposing in the Freedom Camping Bill, but they are a good
step along the way. They are an excellent step along the way of reminding people who
come to New Zealand that we love them —we love people coming to our country; we
love the way they spend money in our count ry and make a contribution to our society—
but please, they must not foul our environment before they go home.
The other point is that unless we get on top of this problem we are in danger of
people coming to New Zealand from, say, Sw eden, parking up agai nst the shores of
Lake W ānaka, seeing the mess left there, and then going back to Sweden and saying
that they loved New Zealand but it is actually not as good as New Zealanders crack it up
to be. We need to be very careful that we maintain New Zealand’s good image.
The reason this bill is so good is that  it is making a stand. Labour members can
lament the fact that the bill will not fix the pr oblem, but it will. It will help to fix the
problem, because we will remind people of their environmental responsibilities. As I
9 Jun 2011 Freedom Camping Bill 19279
say, no single measure will fix this problem. Once again, it is up to individuals to
understand their environmental responsibilities.
In closing, I commend the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkinson, for her
preparedness to act on this issue in adva nce of the Rugby World Cup. I congratulate
Geoff Ensor from the Freedom Camping Forum, who has worked so hard across many
sectors on this bill. I commend this bill to the House.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Freedom Camping Bill be now
read a first time.
Ayes 108
New Zealand National 58; New Zeala nd Labour 42; ACT New Zealand 5; M āori
Party 3.
Noes 10
Green Party 9; Independent: Carter C.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Local Government and Environment Committee.
The House adjourned at 6 p.m.
